text: The Grisons (/ɡriːˈzɒ̃/;[4] French: [ɡʁizɔ̃]) or Graubünden (Swiss Standard German: [ɡraʊˈbʏndn̩] ⓘ),[note 1] more formally the Canton Grisons,[5] is one of the twenty-six cantons of Switzerland. It has eleven districts and its capital is Chur. The German name, Graubünden, means "Grey Leagues," referring to the canton's origin in three local alliances—the Three Leagues. The other native names also reference the Grey League: Grischùn in Sutsilvan, Grischun in the other forms of Romansh, and Grigioni in Italian. Rhaetia is the Latin name for the area. The Alpine ibex is the canton's heraldic symbol. As the largest and easternmost canton of Switzerland, it is one of the three large southern Alpine cantons, along with Valais and Ticino. It is the most diverse canton in terms of natural and cultural geography, encompassing both sides of the Alps and several natural and cultural regions, and is often compared to Switzerland as a whole, earning it the name "Little Switzerland."[6][7] The Grisons is bordered by four Swiss cantons as well as Austria, Italy, and Liechtenstein. It is the only trilingual canton of Switzerland and the only one where Romansh, Switzerland's fourth national language, has official status. Romansh language and culture are an important part of local identity.[9] In 2020, the canton had a population of 200,096.[2] It is the least densely populated canton of Switzerland. The only sizable city is Chur, as the majority of the population lives in mountainous areas, including some of the most remote valleys. One of the birthplaces of winter sports, the canton is a major tourist destination year-round, including numerous Alpine resort towns, notably Davos and St. Moritz. It is also renowned for its extensive narrow-gauge railway network, operated by the Rhaetian Railway, linking the capital with most valleys of the Grisons. Formerly occupied by the Rhaeti, most of the lands of the canton became part of the Roman province Raetia, established in 15 BC, with Curia, a settlement dating back to the Pfyn culture, as its capital. The area later became part of the diocese of Chur. In the late Middle Ages, the League of God's House, the Grey League, and the League of the Ten Jurisdictions were founded. In 1471, an alliance formed the Three Leagues, and by the end of the 15th century, they became allies of the Old Swiss Confederacy. In 1803, the Three Leagues became one of the cantons of the Confederation. The Grisons is Switzerland's largest and easternmost canton. Its geography, marked by the Alps, is complex and includes a wide range of climates and ecosystems. It is one of the three large southern Alpine cantons, along with Ticino and Valais, which include regions on the south side of the Alps. However, unlike those and all other cantons, it fully extends on both sides of the great Alpine barrier, from the northern plains at Maienfeld to the southern plains at Roveredo. A large portion of the canton is neither clearly north nor south of the Alps; it is the Engadin (the "garden of the Inn"), a large inner Alpine valley oriented toward eastern Europe. Therefore, parts of the canton lie in four of the five drainage basins of the country. The north is drained by the Rhine (ending in the North Sea), the south by the Po and Adige through several affluents (Mediterranean Sea), and the Engadin by the Danube through the Inn (Black Sea).[10] The Grisons lies fully within the Alps, with elevations ranging from 260 to 4,049 metres (853 to 13,284 ft). It is both one of the highest and lowest cantons of Switzerland and the second-highest when considering mean elevation. Its topography is extremely rugged, with many of the highest settlements in the country (and Europe) located in the Upper Engadin. There are well over 1,000 summits in the canton.[11] The highest peak is Piz Bernina, closely followed by numerous peaks in the homonymous range. Other prominent mountains include Piz Russein, Piz Kesch, Calanda, Aroser Rothorn, and Rheinwaldhorn (see list of mountains of Graubünden for a more exhaustive list). The canton includes numerous subranges of the Alps other than the Bernina, such as the Albula, Bregaglia, Glarus, Gotthard, Lepontine, Livigno, Plessur, Oberhalbstein, Ortler, Rätikon, Samnaun, Sesvenna, and Silvretta. The northern regions are drained by the Rhine and form an intricate network of valleys. The Rhine is one of the longest rivers in the canton and the only one flowing directly into a sea. Its sources are in the west, forming the Anterior Rhine and the Posterior Rhine, which converge at Reichenau to form the Rhine in the strict sense. After convergence, the valley opens and its floor constitutes the flattest plains of the canton, from Domat/Ems to Fläsch at the St. Gallen border. Around Chur, at the foot of the Calanda, the Rhine changes direction from eastward to northward. The Anterior Rhine and Posterior Rhine have numerous tributaries. The former forms the long and straight Surselva valley, shut off from the lower plains by the Rhine Gorge. Its major tributaries are the Glogn, Valser Rhine, and Rabiusa, forming the Val Lumnezia, Vals Valley, and Safiental. The Posterior Rhine notably collects the waters of the Avers Rhine and the Albula, which in turn collects the waters of the Gelgia and Landwasser. Similarly, the upper portion of the Posterior Rhine is shut off by the Viamala Gorge. After merging with the Albula, the Posterior Rhine forms the wide Domleschg valley until it meets its anterior counterpart. After that, the Rhine collects the waters of the Plessur at Chur, forming the Schanfigg valley, and the Landquart at the homonymous town, forming the Prätigau.[10] The Engadin is entirely drained by the Inn and is the only valley in Switzerland in the Danube basin. The Inn is one of the longest rivers in the canton and forms an almost straight valley from the Maloja Pass to Martina, with a change of direction near Zernez. Despite its length and numerous tributaries, only a few long rivers converge with the Inn: the Flaz (forming the Val Bernina), the Spöl (forming the Val da Spöl), and the Clemgia (forming the Val S-charl). In the lower part of the Engadin is also the side valley of Samnaun. The main passes connecting the Engadin with the northern Grisons are (from west to east): the Julier Pass, the Albula Pass, and the Flüela Pass.[10] The southern valleys are not contiguous and form four distinct regions: the Mesolcina (drained by the Moesa), the Val Bregaglia (drained by the Mera), the Val Poschiavo (drained by the Poschiavino), and the Val Müstair (drained by the Rom). The first three are in the Po basin and the last in the Adige basin. The Mesolcina and Bregaglia are contiguous to the northern regions through the San Bernardino Pass and the Septimer Pass, respectively. The Bregaglia, Poschiavo, and Müstair are contiguous to the Engadin through the Maloja Pass, the Bernina Pass, and the Ofen Pass.[10] Although there are no large bodies of water in the canton, numerous mountain lakes (above 800 m elevation) dot the landscape, some used as reservoirs for hydroelectricity. The largest natural lakes are Lake Sils, Lake Silvaplana, Lago di Poschiavo, and Lake St. Moritz (all in Upper Engadin except Lago di Poschiavo). Artificial lakes are more numerous, with the largest (over 100 ha) being Lago di Livigno, Lago di Lei, Lai da Sontga Maria, Zervreilasee, Lago Bianco, Lai da Marmorera, and Lägh da l'Albigna. The total number of lakes is estimated at 600.[12][note 2] Unlike other large cantons, the Grisons includes very few cities. The largest and capital city is Chur. It is followed by Davos, Landquart, Domat/Ems, and St. Moritz, which are, however, far less populated. The canton is particularly renowned for its numerous Alpine resort towns, notably Davos and St. Moritz, but also Klosters, Arosa, Lenzerheide, Disentis, Flims, Pontresina, and Scuol.[13] The climate diversity is high and comparable to that of Switzerland. In the southernmost and lowest regions, vineyards and olives are grown,[14] while on the highest summits, snow is found year-round. The inner valleys, especially the Engadin, are significantly drier than the north and south sides of the Alps, being sheltered by the high mountains. On the south side, Grono is one of the warmest places in the country with an average of 12.4 °C (54.3 °F), where the nationwide record temperature of 41.5 °C (106.7 °F) was recorded. The southern valleys are also significantly wetter than the rest of the canton (1,476 mm in Grono, 849 mm in Chur, and 705 mm in Scuol). The coldest places are at high elevations, such as on Piz Corvatsch. The Upper Engadin is among the coldest inhabited regions, notably Samedan with an average temperature of 2.0 °C (35.6 °F). The cantonwide record-low temperature of −37.9 °C (−36.2 °F) was recorded there.[15] The low-elevation region of Chur, including the Bündner Herrschaft, experiences less harsh temperatures with an average of 10.0 °C (50.0 °F). The area of the Grisons is 7,105.2 square kilometres (2,743.3 sq mi), 19.2% larger than the canton of Bern, the second largest canton.[16] Only about a third of this area is considered productive land, with forests covering about a fifth of the total area.[16] The canton is almost entirely mountainous and is the most sparsely populated region of the country. In its southeastern part lies the only official Swiss National Park. In its northern part, the mountains were formed as part of the thrust fault declared a geologic UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008 under the name Swiss Tectonic Arena Sardona. Another Biosphere Reserve is the Biosfera Val Müstair adjacent to the Swiss National Park, while Ela Nature Park is one of the regionally supported parks. The Grisons is sometimes included in the larger region of Eastern Switzerland, together with six other cantons. It shares borders with numerous European regions, reflecting its cultural diversity, and is the only canton adjacent to three different countries. On the national level, it shares borders with Uri, Glarus, St. Gallen (essentially across the Glarus Alps), and Ticino (essentially across the Gotthard Massif and the Lepontine Alps, but also at the level of the plain at Roveredo). On the international level, it shares borders with Liechtenstein to the north, the Austrian regions of Vorarlberg and Tyrol to the northeast, and the Italian regions of Trentino-South Tyrol and Lombardy to the east and south.[17] The deep Alpine valleys of the present-day Grisons were originally settled by the Raetians (Rhaeti). In Chur, archaeological evidence of settlement goes back to the Pfyn culture (3900–3500 BC), making the capital one of the oldest settlements in Switzerland. Most of the lands of the canton were once part of the Roman province Raetia, established in 15 BC. The current capital, Chur, was known as Curia in Roman times. The area later became part of the lands of the diocese of Chur. In 1367, the League of God's House (Cadi, Gottes Haus, Ca' di Dio) was founded to resist the rising power of the Bishop of Chur. This was followed by the establishment of the Grey League (Grauer Bund), sometimes called Oberbund, in 1395 in the Upper Rhine valley. The name Grey League is derived from the homespun grey clothes worn by the people and was used exclusively after 16 March 1424.[20] The name of this league later gave its name to the canton of the Grisons. A third league was established in 1436 by the people of ten bailiwicks in the former Toggenburg countship, as the Toggenburg dynasty had become extinct. This league was called the League of the Ten Jurisdictions (Zehngerichtebund). The first step toward the canton of the Grisons was when the League of the Ten Jurisdictions allied with the League of God's House in 1450. In 1471, the two leagues allied with the Grey League. In 1497 and 1498, the Leagues allied with the Old Swiss Confederacy after the Habsburgs acquired the possessions of the extinct Toggenburg dynasty in 1496,[22] siding with the Confederacy in the Swabian War three years later. The Habsburgs were defeated at Calven Gorge and Dornach, helping the Swiss Confederation and the allied leagues of the canton of the Grisons to be recognized. However, the Three Leagues remained a loose association until the Bundesbrief of 23 September 1524.[23] The last traces of the Bishop of Chur's jurisdiction were abolished in 1526. The Musso war of 1520 drove the Three Leagues closer to the Swiss Confederacy. Between 1618 and 1639, it became a battleground during the Bündner Wirren. The Protestant party was supported by France and Venice, while the Catholic party was supported by the Habsburgs in Spain and Austria. Each side sought control of the Grisons to gain control over the important alpine passes. In 1618, the young radical Jörg Jenatsch became a member of the court of 'clerical overseers' and a leader of the anti-Habsburg faction. He supervised the torture to death of the arch-priest Nicolò Rusca of Sondrio. In response, Giacomo Robustelli of the pro-Catholic Planta family raised an army of rebels in the Valtellina. On the evening of 18/19 July 1620, a force of Valtellina rebels supported by Austrian and Italian troops marched into Tirano and began killing Protestants. When they finished in Tirano, they marched to Teglio, Sondrio, and further down the valley, killing every Protestant they found. Between 500[24] and 600[25] people were killed that night and in the following four days. The attack drove nearly all the Protestants out of the valley, prevented further Protestant incursions, and took the Valtellina out of the Three Leagues. In response, in February 1621, Jenatsch led a force of anti-Habsburg troops to attack Rietberg Castle, the home of a leader of the pro-Catholic faction, Pompeius Planta.[26] They surprised Planta and, according to legend, he was killed by Jörg Jenatsch with an axe.[27] The murder of Planta encouraged the Protestant faction, who assembled a poorly led and disorganized army to retake the Valtellina and other subject lands. However, the army fell apart before attacking a single Catholic town.[26] This Protestant invasion provided the Spanish and Austrians with an excuse to invade the Leagues. By the end of October, Spain and Austria had occupied all of the Grisons. The resulting peace treaty of January 1622 forced the Grisons to cede the Müstair, the Lower Engadine, and Prättigau valleys. The treaty also forbade the Protestant religion in these valleys. In response, in 1622, the Prättigau valley rebelled against the Austrians and drove them out of the valley. The Austrians invaded the valley twice more, attempting to reimpose the Catholic faith, in 1623–1624 and 1629–1631.[28] In 1623, the Leagues entered into an alliance with France, Savoy, and Venice. Jürg Jenatsch and Ulysses von Salis used French money to hire an 8,000-man mercenary force.

Of Planta supported the Protestant faction, who assembled a poorly led and disorganized army to retake the Valtellina and other subject lands, but the army collapsed before engaging any Catholic town. This Protestant invasion gave Spain and Austria a pretext to invade the Leagues. By the end of October, Spain and Austria had taken control of all of the Grisons. The peace treaty of January 1622 compelled Grisons to surrender the Müstair, Lower Engadine, and Prättigau valleys, and banned the Protestant religion in these areas. In response, the Prättigau rebelled in 1622 and expelled the Austrians. The Austrians invaded the valley twice more, in 1623–1624 and 1629–1631, attempting to reestablish Catholicism. In 1623, the Leagues allied with France, Savoy, and Venice. Jürg Jenatsch and Ulysses von Salis used French funds to hire an 8,000-man mercenary force to expel the Austrians. The peace treaty of Monzon (5 March 1626) between France and Spain confirmed the political and religious independence of the Valtellina. In 1627, France withdrew from the Valtellina, which was then occupied by Papal troops. Starting in 1631, the League, under the French Duke Henri de Rohan, began expelling Spaniards. However, Richelieu refused to hand the valley over to its residents. When it became clear the French intended to remain permanently in the Leagues without forcing the Valtellina to convert to Protestantism, Jürg Jenatsch (now a mercenary leader) converted to Catholicism in 1635. In 1637, he rebelled and allied with Austria and Spain; his rebellion, along with that of 31 other League officers, forced the French to withdraw without combat. On 24 January 1639, Jürg Jenatsch was killed during Carnival by an unknown attacker dressed as a bear, who may have been a son of Pompeius Planta or an assassin hired by the local aristocracy; according to legend, he was killed by the same axe he used on Pompeius Planta. On 3 September 1639, the Leagues agreed with Spain to bring the Valtellina back under League sovereignty, with the promise to allow free exercise of the Catholic faith. Treaties with Austria in 1649 and 1652 restored the Müstair and Lower Engadine valleys to the authority of the Three Leagues. In 1798, the Grisons' lands became part of the Helvetic Republic as the canton of Raetia, except Valtellina, which was separated in 1797 for joining the Cisalpine Republic. It later became part of the Empire of Austria in 1814 and joined the Kingdom of Italy in 1859. With the Act of Mediation, the "perpetual ally" of Switzerland became a canton in 1803. The canton's constitution dates from 1892 and has undergone about 30 changes in the following century. The arms of the three original leagues were combined into the modern cantonal coat of arms in 1933. The Grand Council (German: Grosser Rat; Italian: Gran Consiglio; Romansh: Cussegl Grond), the legislature, meets in Chur, the cantonal capital. Its 120 members, elected in 39 districts using a majority system, serve four-year terms; the last district elections were in 2014. The cantonal government, exercising executive authority, consists of five members elected by the people for four-year terms, limited to three terms under a majority system. The constitution of the Grisons, last revised on 14 September 2003, states in its preamble that the canton's purpose is to "safeguard freedom, peace, and human dignity, ensure democracy and the Rechtsstaat, promote prosperity and social justice and preserving a sane environment for the future generations, with the intention of promoting trilingualism and cultural variety and conserving them as part of our historical heritage." The constitution allows municipal-level enfranchisement of foreign residents at the discretion of local governments. In 2009, the municipality of Bregaglia became the first to grant voting rights to foreigners. As of January 2017, there are 100 municipalities in the canton (as of January 2025). The inhabitants are called Bündner or (rarely) Grisonians. The population (as of 31 December 2020) is 200,096; as of 2007, it included 28,008 foreigners, or about 14.84% of the total. The main religions are Catholicism and Protestantism, with Roman Catholics forming a slight plurality (47% to 41% Protestant). The Grisons is the only Swiss canton with three official languages: German (74.7%), Romansh (13.9%), and Italian (13.9%), with the remaining 13% speaking another language natively. More Romansh speakers live in the Grisons than in any other canton, though it has become a minority language. Romansh consists of five dialect groups—Sursilvan, Vallader, Puter, Surmiran, and Sutsilvan—with a common written language called Rumantsch Grischun. Romansh has been recognized as one of four "national languages" by the Swiss Federal Constitution since 1938 and was declared an "official language" of the Confederation in 1996, allowing Romansh speakers to use Romansh for federal correspondence and receive responses in Rumantsch Grischun. Romansh has official status at the canton level, with municipalities free to specify their own official languages. Agriculture remains essential for maintaining remote valleys and is supported by national and regional subsidies; eight percent of the population work in agriculture and forestry, where 50 percent of production is certified organic. Agriculture includes forests and mountain pasturage in summer, particularly for cows, sheep, and goats. Since wolves and bears have returned, Maremma Sheepdogs are commonly used. Mountain pastures dominate, but wine production occurs in the Rhine Valley, especially in Fläsch, Maienfeld, Jenins, and Malans, known as the Bündner Herrschaft. In the southern valleys of Mesolcina and Val Poschiavo, corn and chestnut farming are practiced due to the milder climate, and olive trees are grown in Mesolcina. Twenty-four percent of the workforce are employed in industry, while 68 percent work in the service sector. The most industrialized region is Chur, home to Ems-Chemie, a major employer. Tourism is a major economic force, accounting for 14 percent of GDP, concentrated in towns like Davos, Klosters, Lenzerheide, Arosa, Flims, St. Moritz, and Pontresina, which have large ski areas. Numerous other tourist resorts exist, categorized by the official tourist board into "Top – Large – Small and beautiful." St. Moritz is one of the oldest winter sport resorts, popular since 1864; Davos saw its first winter tourists the following year. St. Moritz hosted the 1928 and 1948 Winter Olympics. Summer tourism also contributes significantly, with trekking, mountaineering, and mountain biking as key activities. Business tourism, notably in Davos where the World Economic Forum is traditionally held, is another revenue source. The canton spans both sides of the great Alpine barrier, with many important mountain passes, especially along the north-south axis. Transport has historically been a challenge; Roman-era cart tracks were found on Julier Pass, and Septimer Pass was rebuilt in 1387 for cart use, though it later lost importance and remains in its 1800 form for hikers. Corniche paths were essential over long stretches, and gorges like Viamala posed construction difficulties. The first real roads, 3.7 meters wide, were built across the Alps from around 1816, one of which remains in excellent historical condition. This route lost significance after rail tunnels opened. The last valley connected to the road system was Avers, with its remote hamlet of Juf reached only in 1897. After the Swiss Post expanded its Postal Bus services, motorized traffic became more common; by 1925, there were 250 vehicles in service. The inhabitants eventually accepted individual motor traffic in 1926. In 1967, the San Bernardino road tunnel opened to handle tourism traffic and is now used by heavy goods vehicles, though it is not well suited due to steep gradients. Most other passes are no longer important for goods transport. Unlike Valais and Ticino, the Grisons lacks major railway axes such as the Lötschberg and Gotthard. The only standard gauge railway is in the Rhine Valley, ending at Chur station. Chur has become a major transport hub due to the Rhaetian Railway, which links most regions of the canton. Public transport ensures access to nearly every settlement through an integrated timetable. Even Juf, with only about 30 residents and a European record, is reached five times daily by public transport. The two main transport companies are PostBus and the Rhaetian Railway, which is largely owned by the cantonal government. The Rhaetian Railway operates the largest narrow-gauge network in Switzerland and serves most regions, with branches to Central Switzerland and Italy. It is notably traveled by two of Switzerland’s longest-distance trains: the Glacier Express and the Bernina Express. Swiss Federal Railways extend only a few kilometers into the canton, from Maienfeld, serving Landquart and Chur, where passengers transfer to the Rhaetian Railway and numerous PostBus routes. The Albula Line and the Bernina Railway, the highest and only railway crossing the Alps without a tunnel, are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. In winter, some road passes are closed, while high mountain passes like Julier, Bernina, and Lukmanier remain open (subject to restrictions). As the highest-elevated canton in Switzerland, it hosts vast alpine areas inaccessible by any transport and requiring walking. A large number of cable transport facilities provide access to mountains, with the highest being on Piz Corvatsch. The Engadin valley has its own airport, Samedan Airport, the highest in Switzerland, though there are no scheduled flights. Residents typically use Zurich, Milan’s Malpensa, Linte, or Bergamo airports. The Grisons is culturally the most diverse region of Switzerland, united by a strong mountain culture marked by life in isolated rural communities, notably depicted in Johanna Spyri’s Heidi. Traditional customs include Alpine transhumance in spring and autumn and the Chalandamarz at the end of winter. The canton has a large number of medieval castles and ruins; the most notable in the Engadin is Tarasp, guarding the Inn valley. Many ruins are found in the Domleschg area, and the church of Zillis features a famous 1130/40 romanesque illustrated ceiling now recognized as national heritage. Three World Heritage Sites are located in the canton: the Benedictine Convent of Saint John, the Swiss Tectonic Arena Sardona, and the Rhaetian Railway in the Albula and Bernina Landscapes. The gastronomy of the Grisons is known for Bündnerfleisch (dried beef), often called Grisons Meat, as well as dried sausages (especially Salsiz), speck, and ham. Cheeses are numerous; notable dishes include Capuns (hearty dumplings with meat wrapped in chard leaves, then gratinated with cheese and cream), made primarily in the western part; Maluns (boiled potatoes mixed with flour, fried in butter), typically served with apple compote and local products; and Pizzoccheri (buckwheat noodles with potatoes, vegetables, and cheese), eaten in the Poschiavo valley. The emblematic dessert is the Bündner Nusstorte, a shortcrust pastry filled with caramelized walnuts and honey; a similar pastry with chestnuts, Torta di Castagne, is made in the southern valleys, especially Val Bregaglia. Wines are mainly produced in the Bündner Herrschaft, with 42 types of vines, Pinot Noir being the most popular. Smaller quantities are produced in the southern valleys; the Mesolcina is contiguous with the Ticino wine region, and Poschiavo with the Valtellina wine region. Numerous breweries exist, with the largest located in Chur, Calanda Bräu. Radiotelevisiun Svizra Rumantscha is the Romansh-speaking division of the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation and focuses on the Grisons. Die Südostschweiz (in German) and La Quotidiana (Romansh) are key written media. The Grisons successfully reintroduced the ibex in the early 20th century after it had nearly disappeared from the Alps, except in the Aosta Valley, Italy, Parco Nazionale Gran Paradiso. The bearded vulture and lynx were reintroduced in the 21st century, though the lynx remains rare.
